summary: Sirmilik, "the place of glaciers", spreads across 22,200 square kilometres of northern Baffin Island and Bylot Island, between Pond Inlet and Arctic Bay. Glaciers pour off Bylot's mountains, greater snow geese nest on its south-western plain, and seabirds crowd its cliffs above waters full of narwhals and belugas. Visitors reach it with Inuit outfitters, by snowmobile to the floe edge in spring or by boat to Oliver Sound and Bylot Island in summer.

facts.suggestedTime: A day trip from Pond Inlet to a week or more

story: Sirmilik represents the Eastern Arctic Lowlands natural region, but its name says what dominates the view: Inuktitut for "the place of glaciers". The park is made up of separate parts — Bylot Island, Oliver Sound and the Borden Peninsula on Baffin Island, and a small parcel on Baillarge Bay — joined by the sea. Bylot Island is covered with mountains, icefields, snowfields and steep cliffs, and 16 glaciers flow off it. The Borden Peninsula is a high plateau cut by broad river valleys. Tundra makes up about 60 per cent of the park, and two striking sites of hoodoos, one on Bylot and one on the Borden Peninsula, stand among its rocks.

The sea makes Sirmilik rich. Tallurutiup Imanga (Lancaster Sound), off the park's northern shores, is one of the most productive marine areas in the Canadian Arctic, home to seabirds, walrus, polar bears, seals and whales. More than 70 bird species have been recorded in the park. Thick-billed murres and black-legged kittiwakes nest by the thousand at Cape Hay and Baillarge Bay, and Bylot Island's wet south-western lowlands hold the largest breeding colony of greater snow geese in the Canadian High Arctic, with more than 50,000 birds arriving each year. Narwhals, belugas, seals, caribou, Arctic foxes and wolves complete the picture.

People have hunted here for thousands of years. Pre-Dorset and Dorset people came first; Thule people, the ancestors of today's Inuit, arrived about a thousand years ago, and their sites make up most of those recorded in the park. Many are concentrated around Button Point, at the south-eastern tip of Bylot Island, where a polynya keeps the sea open all year. Robert Bylot and William Baffin sailed into Lancaster Sound in 1616; British whalers reached the area in the 1820s, and for half a century Bylot Island was one of the busiest northern whaling grounds. Inuit of Pond Inlet (Mittimatalik) and Arctic Bay (Ikpiarjuk) still use the park extensively for harvesting and cultural activities.

Joseph-Elzéar Bernier sailed into Eclipse Sound in 1906 and took possession of Bylot Island for Canada. The federal government made Bylot a Migratory Bird Sanctuary in 1965, and in 1988 the Canadian Wildlife Service and Université Laval opened a seasonal research camp there to study the snow geese, work that has since grown to include foxes, lemmings and snowy owls. After the Nunavut Agreement and the 1999 Inuit Impact and Benefit Agreement, Sirmilik was established under the Canada National Parks Act in 2001. It is managed cooperatively by Inuit and Parks Canada, with the Canadian Wildlife Service sharing responsibility for Bylot Island.
howItWorks: Since April 2019 all access to Sirmilik has been designated a hazardous activity, and every visitor must register, attend an orientation and de-register; Inuit exercising their rights under the Nunavut Agreement are not visitors here. Book the orientation with the Parks Canada office in Pond Inlet at least 48 hours ahead by phone or email. Sessions take 60 to 90 minutes, run on weekdays during business hours and do not start after 3:30 pm; if your trip starts in Arctic Bay, plan your flights so you can register in Pond Inlet or Iqaluit first. Within 24 hours of leaving the park, de-register in person or by phone at 867-899-8092; failing to do so starts an investigation. Travel on Inuit-owned land needs permission from the Qikiqtani Inuit Association.

There are no roads or facilities. Licensed outfitters from Pond Inlet or Arctic Bay carry visitors by snowmobile or dog team over the sea ice from late March to early June, and by boat from late July to late September; during break-up and freeze-up no one can reach the park. Bylot Island lies 25 kilometres from Pond Inlet across Eclipse Sound. Aircraft may land only with a permit. Polar bears are most active along the Borden Peninsula coast and the north, west and east coasts of Bylot Island, especially in March and April and from July to October, but can be met anywhere, even on glaciers. Avoid camping near food caches and hunting sites. Only licensed guides or bear monitors with a permit may carry firearms (Inuit excepted), so carry deterrents and know how to use them.

Sirmilik charges the Northern Park Backcountry fees. As Parks Canada listed them in November 2026: CA$17.75 per person for a day excursion (CA$4.75 for educational groups), CA$37.00 per person per night, or CA$259.00 for an annual pass valid in eleven northern parks; youth 17 and under are free. Sport fishing is prohibited. Under the 2016 management plan, parts of the park close seasonally for Inuit harvesting and nesting birds, and Bylot Island's Migratory Bird Sanctuary rules also apply, so ask about current closures at your orientation.

sights.name: Bylot Island
sights.note: The park's largest island, across Eclipse Sound from Pond Inlet: mountains, icefields and 16 glaciers, a Migratory Bird Sanctuary since 1965.

sights.name: Sermilik Glacier
sights.note: A glacier on Bylot Island's south coast, the destination for short boat or snowmobile trips from Pond Inlet for visitors with only a day or two.

sights.name: Aktineq Glacier
sights.note: A Bylot Island glacier crossed on skis in Parks Canada's film on mountain travel in the park. Late March to early June is the season for ski touring.

sights.name: Kangiqluruluk (Oliver Sound)
sights.note: A great fiord south of Pond Inlet with steep cliffs and valley glaciers near the water, ice-free relatively early; good for boating, kayaking, camping and day hikes.

sights.name: Nalluata imanga (Navy Board Inlet)
sights.note: The main sea route to the Borden Peninsula and Cape Hay; glaciers drop abruptly to the shore north of Low Point.

sights.name: Cape Hay
sights.note: Seabird cliffs on Bylot Island's north-west coast. Thick-billed murres and kittiwakes nest here; in summer the colony may be viewed only from a boat.

sights.name: Mala River
sights.note: A Borden Peninsula valley beside a route from Arctic Bay to Pond Inlet proposed for guided snowmobile trips. From 1 June to 31 August, non-motorised travel only.

sights.name: Elwin Inlet
sights.note: An inlet on the Borden Peninsula's north coast near the Baillarge Bay seabird cliffs. The coast south-west of it closes to visitors from 16 June to 31 July for floe-edge harvesting.

entrances: Pond Inlet (Mittimatalik) — the Parks Canada office, and outfitters to Bylot Island, Oliver Sound and Navy Board Inlet
Arctic Bay (Ikpiarjuk) — outfitters to the Borden Peninsula sector
planYourVisit.reservations: Book your orientation at the Pond Inlet office at least 48 hours in advance, and arrange transport with a licensed outfitter; the park office can help with outfitters in Pond Inlet, and the Hamlet Office handles enquiries in Arctic Bay. Guided floe-edge trips run from late April to early June. Ice conditions change every year, so check the likely dates for break-up and freeze-up with the park office before you go.
permits: Mandatory registration and orientation before entering, and de-registration within 24 hours of leaving
Restricted activity permits for landing an aircraft, caches and base camps, drones, commercial filming, research and operating a business
Activities in the Bylot Island Migratory Bird Sanctuary may also need Canadian Wildlife Service authorisation
Permission from the Qikiqtani Inuit Association to travel on Inuit-owned land
camping: No designated campsites: camp anywhere except archaeological sites, special preservation areas, rockfall areas and wildlife habitat such as sedge meadows
No fires; carry a white-gas stove — fuel can be bought in Pond Inlet or Arctic Bay
No camping or other land-based activity in the seabird colonies at Cape Hay and Baillarge Bay
lodging: None in the park; in Pond Inlet the Tununiq Sauniq Hotel and Tamaarvik Territorial Park campground, 5 km from town; in Arctic Bay the Taqqut Inn
The Nattinnak Visitors Centre in Pond Inlet has community visitor information
seasonalClosures: Bylot Island's south-western goose habitat: under the 2016 management plan visitors must avoid it from 1 May to 31 August, and it closes for about two weeks in June for egg harvesting
The centre of the Borden Peninsula sector closes to visitors from 1 June to 31 August for caribou calving and harvesting
The coast south-west of Elwin Inlet closes from 16 June to 31 July
Qinniqtut and the shipwreck at Maud Bight (Umiarjuavinirtalik) are restricted from 1 July to 30 September
During break-up (late June to mid-July) and freeze-up (October to early November) the park cannot be reached

weather: Sirmilik has a polar marine climate of long, cold winters and short, cool summers. The sun hardly sets from May to August and is absent from the sky in December and January. Spring brings strong winds and late summer is often cloudy; snow can fall at any time and whiteouts can occur in any season, and sudden changes can keep boats ashore for days. Late March to early June is the time for ski touring, mountaineering and travel over the sea ice; late July to late September is best for hiking, camping and boating. From November to February, cold, darkness and poor access make travel inadvisable.
directions: Canadian North flies from Montreal, Ottawa and Yellowknife to Iqaluit, and on to Pond Inlet and Arctic Bay; Kenn Borek Air and Air Nunavut offer charters. From either community, licensed outfitters take you to the park by boat or snowmobile, depending on the season — Bylot Island is 25 kilometres across Eclipse Sound from Pond Inlet. Weather can delay northern flights, so leave room in your plans, and allow four to six extra weeks for supplies shipped from abroad to clear customs.

chronology.text: Pre-Dorset people, the earliest known on Baffin Island, are living on the island.
Thule people, ancestors of today's Inuit, arrive in the eastern Arctic.
Robert Bylot and William Baffin sail into Lancaster Sound.
British whalers begin hunting bowhead in the area; Bylot Island becomes a major whaling ground.
Joseph-Elzéar Bernier takes possession of Bylot Island for Canada.
The Hudson's Bay Company arrives at Pond Inlet.
Bylot Island is designated a Migratory Bird Sanctuary.
The Canadian Wildlife Service and Université Laval set up a seasonal research camp on Bylot Island.
The Inuit Impact and Benefit Agreement for Auyuittuq, Quttinirpaaq and Sirmilik is signed.
Sirmilik National Park is established under the Canada National Parks Act.
The park's management plan sets out its zoning and seasonal closures.
Access to the park is designated hazardous and visitor registration made mandatory.

safety: Polar bears can be met anywhere, at any time; take particular care on the coasts of Bylot Island and the Borden Peninsula, keep watch, and never sleep in the open.
River crossings are the biggest summer hazard: glacier-fed rivers rise through the day and after rain. Be prepared to wait hours or days.
Arctic water kills quickly. Sea kayaking is only for very experienced paddlers with dry suits, in certain areas; wind, floating ice and tides can change conditions fast.
On snowmobile and qamutik trips, sea ice thins early near river mouths and in narrow channels; ask park staff where the thin ice is.
Rescue is limited and aircraft can be grounded for days; carry a satellite phone and spare power. Emergency line: 1-780-852-3100.
regulations: Registration and orientation before entering and de-registration within 24 hours of leaving are mandatory.
No fires, no recreational drones and no sport fishing; firearms only under permit (Inuit excepted).
Pets and sled dogs must be kept under physical control at all times.
Seabird colonies may be viewed only from boats in the ice-free season, and Canadian Wildlife Service rules apply in the Bylot Island sanctuary.
Do not disturb wildlife or collect plants, rocks, fossils, antlers or artefacts; leave archaeological features untouched and build no cairns.
